answers.answer: In SCOP 1.75, PDB 1acc (anthrax protective antigen, Bacillus anthracis) chain A was a single whole-chain domain, d1acca_ (sunid 43828, region "A:"), classified in class f (membrane and cell-surface proteins and peptides) as f.11.1.1 (species-level node under sunid 56991). In SCOPe 2.08 (current release; periodic update 2026-08-16) the same chain is split into two domains: d1acca2 (sunid 238522, A:14-225, b.179.1.1; the N-terminal region, species Bacillus anthracis, with a PA14 family node in the all-beta class b) and d1acca1 (sunid 238521, A:226-735, f.60.1.1; the C-terminal region, family 'Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like', species Anthrax bacillus, TaxId 1392). So one single-domain/whole-chain assignment became two domains with different classes (b and f), folds and superfamilies, and the old f.11 identifier no longer describes the chain. I verified the 1.75 and 2.08 domain lists through the API; I did not independently trace intermediate releases (2.01–2.07) or pull the SCOPe changelog, so I can't say in which release the split happened. Name caveat: the superfamily/fold names of f.60/b.179 beyond the family/domain labels above come from the API labels I retrieved; I did not check them against a separate source. Interpretation: a PDB chain is not the same as an evolutionary module. SCOP domains are defined by structural and evolutionary evidence, and a multi-domain chain can contain regions with different ancestry; an early whole-chain assignment can be a placeholder that later curation, with more structures and sequence relatives, resolves into separate domains. Superfamily and family membership (shared common ancestry) applies per domain, not per chain, and the two segments of 1acc A carry different evolutionary relationships (the PA14-type β domain at residues 14-225 versus the C-terminal region at 226-735). Domain boundaries themselves are curatorial judgments and can be revised between releases, so a domain ID/range is release-specific. Implications for homology searches: (1) Do not assign one fold/superfamily to a whole chain or use the chain-level 1.75 class f.11 label; split the query into domains first (use the current SCOPe domain ranges, e.g. A:14-225 and A:226-735) and search each separately. (2) Hits to only one domain support homology only for that segment; they do not justify transferring function, fold or family to the rest of the chain, and a hit to one domain says nothing about the other. (3) When building benchmarks, templates or non-redundant sets, use the same release for both labels and boundaries, and map old IDs (d1acca_, sunid 43828) to the new ones by residue range rather than assuming identity; old labels can leak or mislabel. (4) Domain-architecture/co-occurrence matters: the presence of a domain in a different multi-domain context does not imply homology of the full-length proteins. (5) Use sequence/structure evidence (e.g., E-values, alignment coverage, structural superposition) per domain, and check the release when reporting results; sequence similarity of a homolog should be judged on the covered region only. Limits: a shared SCOPe superfamily indicates probable common ancestry, not identical function, and a family assignment gives only stronger (not guaranteed) functional inference.
